properties.statement:
AN UNDECLARED PROPERTY, ONCE WRITTEN, CANNOT BE REMOVED — and I found out by writing 16,000 characters into one.

⭐ CAUGHT BY THE FEATURE BUILT FOR IT, ON ITS FIRST LIVE USE, ON ITS AUTHOR. Hours after `create_node` gained `undeclared` (#213), the very next ChangeEvent I wrote came back carrying `"undeclared": ["description"]`. `ChangeEvent` declares `name`, `change_type`, `subject`, `summary` (fulltext) and `rationale` — there is NO `description`. I had been writing long accounts into an invented field all day.

MEASURED: SIX ChangeEvents carry it, all mine from 2026-08-16, roughly 16,000 characters between them. And the cost is not cosmetic — THE CONTENT IS EFFECTIVELY UNFINDABLE. Searching a phrase that appears ONLY in one of those descriptions ranked its node THIRD, below nodes that merely matched on `name`; `summary` is declared `fulltext: true` and `description` is not indexed for this type at all. So the reasoning is stored, readable if you already know the id, and invisible to the search that exists to find it.

⚠️ AND HERE IS THE DEFECT THAT MAKES IT WORTH A NODE RATHER THAN AN APOLOGY: THERE IS NO WAY TO DELETE A PROPERTY. `create_node` MERGES — what you pass overwrites, what you omit survives — which is correct and load-bearing (BL-46), and it means a property can be overwritten but never removed. The only route to a clean node is `delete_node` + recreate, which destroys every edge attached to it. ⇒ So the honest repair for a typo'd property is either to leave it, or to accept collateral damage that is worse than the typo. The near-duplicate guard, the edge-endpoint guard and now the undeclared-property report all catch mistakes at the WRITE; nothing can undo one.

WHAT IS OWED, and deliberately not done in the change that found it: the six should have their content moved to `summary`, where it is indexed. That is ~16 KB re-passed through tool calls and it duplicates rather than moves, since `description` cannot be dropped — the least-bad form is to set `summary` to the text and overwrite `description` with a short pointer. It was left because it is cleanup, not the requirement being built, and doing it half-way is worse than doing it deliberately.

NOT ESTABLISHED: whether other node types are being written with an undeclared `description` the same way (only ChangeEvent was checked), and whether a `delete_property` operation is wanted at all — it is a small hole in an otherwise deliberate merge contract, and adding a way to remove things has its own risks.
